subject: COM

task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 08 Computing, and keep one piece of evidence for each.

modules.title: Databases and queries
modules.outcome: create tables and write simple queries
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Databases and queries', taught in a way that is with notes, a worked line and a self-mark. The target is clear: create tables and write simple queries. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: See it: watch or try the skill in 'Databases and queries' on a teacher screen or a safe device.
Name the parts: write the key words and what each part does.
Use it: create tables and write simple queries. Save your work in a named file or folder.
Test and fix: run it, find one fault, correct it, and note what you changed.
modules.example: Solved: Table Students: ID, Name, Class. Query: SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Class = '7B'; lists the names in 7B. Method: Model run for 'Databases and queries'. Goal in one sentence. Plan: list the steps in order before touching the device. Do: follow the plan, saving after each step. Test: try normal input and one unusual input. Fix: change one thing and test again. Share: show a partner and explain it. What a good answer looks like: it works for normal input, steps match the plan, and the learner can explain each part. Online safety rules apply at all times.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Create tables and write simple queries: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Create a table: A learner opens a database tool and types: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, grade INTEGER, score INTEGER); The tool replies that the table was created, with four columns and no rows yet.

Step 2, Insert data: He types INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Learner 1',8,72),(2,'Learner 2',8,91),(3,'Learner 3',8,65),(4,'Learner 4',8,88); The tool reports 4 rows added. Text values are in quotes, numbers are not.
Step 3, Select all: SELECT * FROM students; shows all 4 rows and 4 columns. The star means every column. The learner checks the output matches what he typed, which verifies the insert.

Step 4, Filter and order: SELECT name, score FROM students WHERE score >= 80 ORDER BY score DESC; returns two rows: Learner 2 91 first, then Learner 4 88. Learner 1 at 72 and Learner 3 at 65 fail the WHERE test.
Step 5, Aggregate: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students; returns 4. SELECT AVG(score) FROM students; returns 79.0 because 72 plus 91 plus 65 plus 88 is 316, and 316 divided by 4 is 79.
Step 6, Update and check: UPDATE students SET score = 70 WHERE id = 3; changes Learner 3 from 65 to 70. Running AVG again gives 80.25, since the total is now 321 and 321 divided by 4 is 80.25.

Your turn: Table books(id, title, pages) with (1,'Sea',120),(2,'Sky',200),(3,'Sand',80). List books over 100 pages shortest first, and count them. Model answer: SELECT title, pages FROM books WHERE pages > 100 ORDER BY pages ASC; gives Sea 120, Sky 200; adding WHERE pages > 100 to COUNT(*) gives 2.

Plan: list the steps in order before touching the device. Do: follow the plan, saving after each step. Test: try normal input and one unusual input. Fix: change one thing and test again. Share: show a partner and explain it. What a good answer looks like: it works for normal input, steps match the plan, and the learner can explain each part. Online safety rules apply at all times.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Break a task into functions and use lists: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Break the task into parts. Task: report on five test marks. Parts: find the average, find the highest mark and count how many passed with 50 or more. Each part becomes a function, a named block of code that can be reused and tested on its own.

Step 2, Store the data in a list: marks = [56, 72, 45, 88, 67]. Counting starts at 0, so marks[0] is 56 and marks[-1] is 67. marks[1:3] is the slice [72, 45]. len(marks) is 5. A list keeps related values together under one name.

Step 3, Write a function with a parameter and a return value. def average(items): return sum(items) / len(items). Calling average(marks) gives 328 / 5 = 65.6. The word return sends the answer back. The max(marks) built-in gives 88.

Step 4, Write a function with a loop and a decision. def count_pass(items, limit): count = 0, for x in items: if x >= limit: count += 1, then return count. Calling count_pass(marks, 50) returns 4, because 45 is the only mark below 50.

Step 5, Change the list and run the functions again. marks.append(90) adds a sixth mark. Now len(marks) is 6 and average(marks) is 418 / 6 = 69.67. The functions work with the longer list without any rewriting, which is the benefit of breaking a task into functions.
Step 6, Your turn: temps = [21, 25, 19, 30, 24]. Write a function that counts the temperatures above 22, and find the average. Answer: count is 3 (25, 30 and 24), and the average is 119 / 5 = 23.8.

modules.standard: Style a multi-page site: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, Plan the site: A learner builds a 2-page site for a class garden club: index.html (home) and about.html (members), plus one shared style.css. Keeping all three in one folder makes links simple.

Step 2, Shared navigation: In both pages she puts
Home About
inside the body. Clicking Home or About now moves between the pages from either one.
Step 3, Link the stylesheet: In the head of both pages she adds <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">. Without this line the CSS file would be ignored, so every page that wants the style needs it.

Step 4, Write CSS: In style.css she writes body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; background-color: #f4f4f4; } and h1 { color: #036; } and nav a { margin-right: 12px; color: #0a6; }. Each rule has a selector and property: value; pairs.

Step 5, Check both pages: She refreshes index.html and about.html. Both have a light grey background, dark blue headings, and green links spaced 12 pixels apart. One change in style.css affects both pages, which saves time.

Step 6, Fix an error: The About page is not styled because she wrote href="styles.css" with an extra s. She changes it to style.css, refreshes, and the style appears. Matching the exact file name is vital.

Your turn: Add a third page contact.html with the same style and nav. Model answer: copy the head including <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">, add a Contact link in the nav of all 3 pages, and check each page shows the grey background.

modules.example: Solved: AI can be wrong. Check one fact from a second source. Never type personal details into an AI tool. Method: Model run for 'Safe use of artificial intelligence tools'. Goal in one sentence. Plan: list the steps in order before touching the device. Do: follow the plan, saving after each step. Test: try normal input and one unusual input. Fix: change one thing and test again. Share: show a partner and explain it. What a good answer looks like: it works for normal input, steps match the plan, and the learner can explain each part. Online safety rules apply at all times.
modules.activity: About 30 to 40 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a worked task and a corrected copy.
modules.standard: Use AI tools responsibly and check their answers: at least 8 of 10 marks on a short task, with one line of reasoning for each answer.
steps: Step 1, The task: A learner asks an AI tool, 'What is 15 percent of 240?' The tool replies, '15 percent of 240 is 34.' The learner remembers that AI tools can sound confident but still be wrong, so he plans to check.

Step 2, Check by calculation: He works it out himself. 10 percent of 240 is 24 and 5 percent is 12, so 15 percent is 24 plus 12, which is 36. The tool was wrong by 2. Only the calculation can prove the correct answer.

Step 3, Ask it to show reasoning: The learner writes, 'Show your steps.' The tool now says 240 times 0.15 equals 36. A second try with working gives the right result, but he does not trust it until he has also checked it by hand.

Step 4, Check a source claim: The tool says a book called 'The Desert Rain' by a named author proves a fact. The learner searches the school library catalogue and finds no such book. He treats this as an invented source and does not cite it.

Step 5, Protect privacy: The learner was about to paste his full name, home address and a class photo into the tool. He stops, because anything typed may be stored. He removes the personal details and asks only about the maths.

Step 6, Use honestly: His homework is to write about deserts. He uses the AI for ideas, writes the answer in his own words, checks two facts in a trusted encyclopedia, and tells his teacher he used AI for ideas.

Your turn: An AI says the capital of a country is a city you doubt. What do you do? Model answer: check a trusted atlas or government site, trust the match with two reliable sources, and note that the AI was unreliable.
